answer: A practical anti-Sybil defense requires every new agent to complete a unique memory-hard puzzle tied to a hardware-bound nonce that expires quickly. The puzzle difficulty rises with the number of recent claims from similar environments, so an attacker trying to flood the network with fake agents immediately faces a gale of escalating compute expense. That cost echoes across every additional identity they create, forcing them to wander among ever-larger clusters of real machines just to maintain the illusion of many distinct participants.
